intuition: Classification answers 'what is in this image?'. Detection answers 'what, and roughly where (a box)?'. SEGMENTATION answers 'what is at every single pixel?' - the finest-grained visual output, and the one that matters when a box is not good enough: a surgical tool overlapping tissue, a drivable-road boundary, the exact extent of a tumour. The task splits into three flavours that are constantly confused in interviews, so it is worth fixing them precisely. SEMANTIC segmentation labels each pixel with a CLASS ('person', 'road') and does not distinguish individuals - three overlapping people are one 'person' region. INSTANCE segmentation separates individual OBJECTS ('person 1', 'person 2') but typically ignores amorphous background regions like sky or road. PANOPTIC segmentation unifies them: every pixel gets a class, and every pixel belonging to a countable 'thing' also gets an instance id, while 'stuff' classes (sky, road, grass) are labelled but not instanced.

Architecturally the semantic problem is the encoder-decoder problem of the previous lesson: you must downsample to get receptive field and semantics, then recover resolution to make per-pixel predictions. Three families of answers exist. FCN convolutionalized a classifier and upsampled its coarse predictions. U-NET added concatenating skips at every scale, which is what makes boundaries sharp. DEEPLAB took the other route - stop downsampling early, use DILATED (atrous) convolutions to grow the receptive field at 1/8 resolution, and capture multi-scale context with ASPP. All three are ways of paying back the spatial precision that downsampling destroyed.

Instance segmentation needs something extra, because 'which pixels belong to the same object' is not expressible as a per-pixel class. The dominant answer for years was TWO-STAGE / detect-then-segment: Mask R-CNN finds boxes, then predicts a binary mask inside each box - simple, accurate, and it inherits detection's machinery (NMS, RoIAlign). More recent work reframes ALL THREE tasks as one: predict a set of binary MASKS with associated class labels (DETR-style set prediction, then MaskFormer/Mask2Former), which removes the box scaffolding and unifies semantic, instance, and panoptic under a single formulation. Meanwhile SAM showed that class-agnostic, promptable segmentation can be trained at foundation-model scale and used zero-shot - which has already changed how annotation pipelines work.

math.h: IoU and Dice: the two metrics, and how they relate
paras: Both measure overlap between a predicted mask P and ground truth G, and both are RATIOS, which is why they survive the extreme class imbalance that makes pixel accuracy useless. IoU (Jaccard) is the stricter of the two - it always sits at or below Dice - and is the standard for reporting (mean IoU over classes, mIoU). Dice (equivalently F1 over pixels) is the standard for the LOSS, because its gradient behaves better.
math.tex: \mathrm{IoU} = \frac{|P \cap G|}{|P \cup G|} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP + FN}, \qquad \mathrm{Dice} = \frac{2|P \cap G|}{|P| + |G|} = \frac{2TP}{2TP + FP + FN} = \frac{2\,\mathrm{IoU}}{1 + \mathrm{IoU}}
math.texNote: The last identity means the two always agree on ranking, but Dice reports a higher number (IoU 0.5 = Dice 0.67). Both ignore true negatives entirely - which is exactly why they, and not accuracy, are the right metrics when 99% of pixels are background.

math.h: Soft Dice loss and the Tversky generalization
paras: To use Dice as a LOSS you replace the hard mask with the predicted PROBABILITY map, which makes it differentiable. Tversky generalizes it with separate weights on false positives and false negatives, letting you encode the real cost asymmetry - in medical work, missing a lesion (FN) is usually far worse than flagging extra tissue (FP), so beta > alpha.
math.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}} = 1 - \frac{2\sum_i p_i g_i + \epsilon}{\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i + \epsilon}, \qquad \mathrm{Tversky} = \frac{TP}{TP + \alpha\,FP + \beta\,FN}
math.texNote: p_i = predicted probability, g_i = ground-truth indicator, epsilon smooths the empty-mask case. alpha = beta = 0.5 recovers Dice. In practice the standard objective is a weighted sum of cross-entropy (stable per-pixel gradients) and Dice (imbalance-invariant, optimizes the reported metric).

code.h: IoU, Dice, and the metrics that actually matter
paras: Compute these from a confusion matrix rather than ad hoc, so per-class numbers and the mean come out consistently. The final lines are the point of the snippet: pixel accuracy is a meaningless number on imbalanced masks, and the mean over classes can hide catastrophic failure on a rare class.
code.code:
import numpy as np

def confusion(pred, target, n_classes):
    k = (target >= 0) & (target < n_classes)
    return np.bincount(n_classes * target[k].astype(int) + pred[k],
                       minlength=n_classes**2).reshape(n_classes, n_classes)

def metrics(cm):
    tp = np.diag(cm)
    fp, fn = cm.sum(0) - tp, cm.sum(1) - tp
    iou  = tp / np.maximum(tp + fp + fn, 1)
    dice = 2 * tp / np.maximum(2 * tp + fp + fn, 1)
    return iou, dice, tp.sum() / cm.sum()

cm = confusion(pred, target, n_classes=3)          # classes: background, road, pedestrian
iou, dice, pix_acc = metrics(cm)
print('per-class IoU :', iou.round(3))             # [0.982 0.874 0.412]
print('mIoU          :', iou.mean().round(3))      # 0.756
print('pixel accuracy:', round(pix_acc, 3))        # 0.971  <- useless: background dominates
# The rare class (pedestrian, IoU 0.41) is the one that matters and the one the
# mean hides. ALWAYS report per-class numbers, not just the mean.
code.caption: Metrics from a confusion matrix: per-class IoU/Dice plus pixel accuracy. Pixel accuracy reads 0.971 while the safety-critical class sits at IoU 0.41 - the standard demonstration that aggregate metrics launder failures on rare classes.

code.h: Dilated convolution: receptive field without losing resolution
paras: The DeepLab trick in code. A stack with increasing dilation rates covers a large context at full resolution, and ASPP runs several rates in PARALLEL so the network sees multiple scales at once. The mixed rates are deliberate: repeating one rate samples a sparse lattice and produces gridding artifacts.
code.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class ASPP(nn.Module):
    """Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling: parallel dilated convs + image-level context."""
    def __init__(self, cin, cout=256, rates=(1, 6, 12, 18)):
        super().__init__()
        self.branches = nn.ModuleList([
            nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(cin, cout, 3 if r > 1 else 1,
                                    padding=r if r > 1 else 0, dilation=r, bias=False),
                          nn.BatchNorm2d(cout), nn.ReLU(inplace=True)) for r in rates])
        self.pool = nn.Sequential(nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1),        # global context branch
                                  nn.Conv2d(cin, cout, 1, bias=False),
                                  nn.BatchNorm2d(cout), nn.ReLU(inplace=True))
        self.project = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(cout * (len(rates) + 1), cout, 1, bias=False),
                                     nn.BatchNorm2d(cout), nn.ReLU(inplace=True))

    def forward(self, x):
        feats = [b(x) for b in self.branches]
        g = nn.functional.interpolate(self.pool(x), size=x.shape[-2:], mode='bilinear',
                                      align_corners=False)
        return self.project(torch.cat(feats + [g], dim=1))

# a 3x3 conv with dilation r has the receptive field of a (2r+1) kernel at 9 weights:
for r in (1, 6, 12, 18):
    print(f'rate {r:2d} -> effective kernel {2*r+1:2d}x{2*r+1:<2d} with 9 weights')
code.caption: ASPP: parallel 3x3 convolutions at several dilation rates plus a global-pooling branch, concatenated and projected. Dilation buys receptive field with no extra parameters and no resolution loss - the alternative to U-Net's downsample-then-upsample.

useCases: Autonomous driving and robotics perception: drivable-area and lane segmentation, free-space estimation, and per-pixel obstacle masks, where a bounding box around an irregular object (a curb, a puddle, a trailer) is not an actionable representation.

Medical imaging: organ and lesion delineation for volumetry, radiotherapy planning, and surgical navigation - the domain where segmentation is most mature (U-Net/nnU-Net) and where the evaluation unit is often the LESION rather than the pixel.

Photo and video editing: portrait mode, background replacement, sky replacement, and rotoscoping are all instance or matting-style segmentation, usually with a hard real-time budget and a strong requirement on boundary quality (hair, transparency).

Remote sensing and science: land-cover classification, crop and deforestation monitoring, cell counting in microscopy, and defect maps in industrial inspection - all large-image dense prediction, usually tiled and stitched, where class imbalance is extreme.
pitfalls: Reporting pixel accuracy or only the MEAN IoU: with a dominant background, accuracy is meaningless, and mIoU averages away catastrophic failure on the rare class you actually care about. Report per-class IoU, and stratify by object size (Dice punishes small objects far more for the same absolute error).

Confusing the three tasks: semantic = class per pixel (no instances), instance = separate objects (usually 'things' only), panoptic = both, with 'stuff' classes labelled but not instanced. Using an instance metric (mask AP) for a semantic model, or mIoU for an instance model, is a common and revealing mistake.

Ignoring boundary quality: region metrics are nearly blind to edge errors on large objects, so a model can score well on mIoU and still look wrong. Add boundary-F1 at a tolerance, or 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance, when edges matter.

Uniform dilation stacks: repeating one dilation rate samples a sparse lattice and causes GRIDDING artifacts (some pixels never contribute). Use mixed/increasing rates (hybrid dilated convolution) or parallel rates as in ASPP.

Tiling large images without overlap: predictions degrade near tile borders because context is missing, producing visible seams. Use overlapping tiles with weighted blending (and remember the receptive field determines the required overlap).

connections.text: U-Net is the standard architecture for this task - that lesson covers the encoder-decoder mechanics, skip connections, and upsampling operators this one applies.
Instance segmentation is largely detection plus a mask head: Mask R-CNN inherits region proposals, RoIAlign, and NMS from the detection stack.
Real-time segmentation on edge hardware depends on efficient backbones and dilation instead of heavy decoders - dense prediction is where the FLOP budget bites hardest.
Segmentation masks are an extreme imbalance problem (often <1% foreground), which is why Dice/Tversky/focal losses and foreground-biased patch sampling are standard rather than optional.

quickGrind.q: What is semantic segmentation?
quickGrind.a: Assigning a class label to every pixel, without distinguishing individual objects - three overlapping people form one 'person' region.

quickGrind.q: What is instance segmentation?
quickGrind.a: Separating individual object instances with their own masks ('person 1', 'person 2'), typically only for countable 'things', not amorphous 'stuff'.

quickGrind.q: What is panoptic segmentation?
quickGrind.a: The unification: every pixel gets a class, and pixels belonging to 'things' also get an instance id, while 'stuff' classes are labelled but not instanced.

quickGrind.q: What is IoU?
quickGrind.a: Intersection over union: TP/(TP+FP+FN). Mean IoU over classes (mIoU) is the standard semantic-segmentation metric.

quickGrind.q: How do IoU and Dice relate?
quickGrind.a: Dice = 2*IoU/(1+IoU), so Dice is always >= IoU and they rank identically. IoU is standard for reporting; Dice is standard for the loss.

quickGrind.q: Why not pixel accuracy?
quickGrind.a: Background typically dominates - predicting all background can score 97-99% while finding nothing. IoU/Dice ignore true negatives, which is why they work.

quickGrind.q: What is a dilated (atrous) convolution?
quickGrind.a: A convolution with gaps between kernel taps: a 3x3 with rate r covers a (2r+1)x(2r+1) region using only 9 weights, growing the receptive field with no downsampling.

quickGrind.q: What is ASPP?
quickGrind.a: Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling - parallel dilated convolutions at several rates plus a global-pooling branch, concatenated to capture multi-scale context (DeepLab).

quickGrind.q: How does Mask R-CNN work?
quickGrind.a: Faster R-CNN (region proposals + box refinement) plus a small FCN mask head predicting a binary mask per RoI, with RoIAlign replacing RoIPool to avoid quantization misalignment.

quickGrind.q: What is RoIAlign and why does it matter?
quickGrind.a: Bilinear sampling of RoI features without rounding coordinates to the feature grid. RoIPool's rounding misaligns masks by up to a stride - fatal for pixel-accurate masks, minor for boxes.

quickGrind.q: What is the mask AP metric?
quickGrind.a: Average precision computed with mask IoU instead of box IoU, averaged over IoU thresholds 0.5:0.05:0.95 - the standard instance-segmentation metric (COCO).

quickGrind.q: What is SAM?
quickGrind.a: Segment Anything - a promptable, class-agnostic segmentation foundation model (ViT encoder + light mask decoder) trained on ~1B masks, used zero-shot and to bootstrap annotation.

standard.q: Compare semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation: the task definitions, the architectures, and the metrics for each.
standard.a: TASK DEFINITIONS. SEMANTIC segmentation assigns a class to every pixel with NO notion of individual objects: a crowd of people is one connected 'person' region. Formally it is per-pixel classification over K classes. INSTANCE segmentation identifies individual OBJECT instances and gives each its own binary mask, so overlapping people become person-1, person-2, person-3. It is defined only over countable 'things' (person, car, dog) and traditionally ignores 'stuff' (sky, road, grass) - and note that instance masks may OVERLAP, since two objects can occlude each other and each gets its full predicted extent. PANOPTIC segmentation unifies both under one constraint: every pixel is assigned exactly one (class, instance-id) pair, where instance-id is meaningful for things and null for stuff - so the output is a NON-OVERLAPPING complete partition of the image, which is the representation you actually want for scene understanding. ARCHITECTURES. For SEMANTIC: fully-convolutional encoder-decoders. FCN (convolutionalize a classifier, upsample, add a couple of skips) started it; U-NET added concatenating skips at every scale for sharp boundaries and dominates in medical/low-data settings; DEEPLAB kept resolution at 1/8 with DILATED convolutions and added ASPP for multi-scale context plus a light decoder (v3+); PSPNet used pyramid pooling for global context; HRNet maintained high resolution throughout in parallel branches; SegFormer and Swin-based models replaced the backbone with transformers. For INSTANCE: historically TWO-STAGE detect-then-segment - Mask R-CNN adds a small FCN mask head to Faster R-CNN, predicting a binary mask per region proposal, with RoIAlign for pixel-accurate feature extraction. One-stage variants (YOLACT, SOLO, CondInst) trade some accuracy for speed by predicting masks directly without proposals. For PANOPTIC: originally two branches (a semantic head plus an instance head) fused by heuristics resolving overlaps - which was ugly and error-prone. The modern answer is MASK CLASSIFICATION: MaskFormer/Mask2Former predict a SET of N binary masks each with a class label (following DETR's set-prediction formulation with Hungarian matching), which expresses all three tasks in one architecture - semantic segmentation is just the case where masks of the same class get merged. This unification is the most important recent conceptual shift in the area, and being able to state it well is what separates a current answer from a 2018 answer. METRICS. SEMANTIC: mean IoU over classes (mIoU) is the standard; also frequency-weighted IoU, and boundary-F1 when edge quality matters. Report PER-CLASS IoU, because the mean hides rare-class failure. INSTANCE: mask AP - average precision using mask IoU to decide matches, averaged over IoU thresholds 0.5 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05 (COCO convention), plus AP_small/medium/large. Note this is a DETECTION-style metric: it cares about ranking and about matching whole objects, not per-pixel accuracy. PANOPTIC: PQ (Panoptic Quality) = SQ x RQ, where segmentation quality SQ is the mean IoU of matched segments and recognition quality RQ is the F1 over segment matches at IoU > 0.5 - elegantly factorizing 'did you find the right segments' from 'how well did you delineate them'. HOW TO CHOOSE THE TASK, which is the practically important question: if you only need to know what material or region is where (drivable area, tissue type, land cover), semantic is cheaper to label and to model. If you need to COUNT, TRACK, or reason about individual objects (count cells, track pedestrians, pick one item), you need instances. If you need a complete, non-overlapping scene description (robot navigation, AR occlusion), you need panoptic. Labelling cost differs sharply too - instance masks are far more expensive to annotate than semantic masks, which is a real project consideration.

deepDive.q: Why is instance segmentation harder than semantic segmentation, and why did the field move from detect-then-segment to mask classification?
deepDive.a: WHY IT IS HARDER, in three specific ways. (1) THE OUTPUT SPACE IS NOT FIXED. Semantic segmentation has a fixed output shape: H x W x K logits, one distribution per pixel, which maps perfectly onto a convolutional network. Instance segmentation must output a VARIABLE NUMBER of masks - three people in one image, twelve in another - so there is no fixed tensor to regress. Every design must answer 'how do I emit a variable-length set?'. (2) INSTANCE IDENTITY IS PERMUTATION-INVARIANT. There is no canonical ordering of instances, so the loss cannot simply compare output i to ground-truth i; it needs a MATCHING between predictions and ground truth (greedy IoU matching in older methods, Hungarian bipartite matching in set-prediction methods). That is a fundamentally different training objective from per-pixel cross-entropy. (3) THE INFORMATION IS NON-LOCAL. Whether two pixels belong to the same instance can depend on evidence far away - two disconnected patches of a partly occluded car are one instance, while two adjacent pixels on touching cars are different instances. A per-pixel classifier cannot express this with any local decision rule, which is exactly why naive 'predict an instance id per pixel' approaches fail. THE DETECT-THEN-SEGMENT ERA. Mask R-CNN's answer was to borrow detection's solution to the variable-set problem: propose regions, then treat each region independently as a small binary segmentation problem. This works well (it was state of the art for years and remains a strong, well-supported baseline) and it neatly sidesteps the identity problem, since each RoI IS an instance by construction. But it inherits detection's baggage: hand-designed ANCHORS with their scale/aspect hyperparameters, NON-MAXIMUM SUPPRESSION as a non-differentiable post-processing step that fails on heavily overlapping objects, a fixed low mask resolution inside each RoI (28x28 in Mask R-CNN, then resized - so large objects get coarse masks), and a hard separation from semantic segmentation that forces panoptic systems to fuse two incompatible outputs with heuristics. WHY MASK CLASSIFICATION WON. The reframing (MaskFormer, Mask2Former, following DETR) is: instead of classifying PIXELS, predict a fixed number N of (mask, class) pairs, where each mask is a soft binary map over the whole image and the class may be 'no object'. Training uses Hungarian matching between the N predictions and the ground-truth segments, then a per-pair mask loss plus classification loss. The advantages are substantial. (a) IT UNIFIES ALL THREE TASKS: semantic segmentation falls out by merging same-class masks, instance segmentation by keeping them separate, panoptic by resolving overlaps with a simple argmax - ONE architecture, one training recipe, three tasks, which was previously impossible. (b) NO ANCHORS, NO NMS: set prediction with bipartite matching makes duplicates unnecessary to suppress, because the matching loss already penalizes them - so the pipeline becomes end-to-end differentiable. (c) MASKS ARE FULL-RESOLUTION, not confined to a box, so objects with irregular or disconnected extents are representable, and an object is not forced to fit a rectangle. (d) IT SEPARATES 'WHAT' FROM 'WHERE' cleanly: each query learns to attend to one segment and to name it, which turns out to be a better factorization than per-pixel labelling. Mask2Former added masked attention (attention restricted to the predicted mask region) and multi-scale features, which fixed the slow convergence and small-object weakness of the first version, and it beat specialized architectures on all three tasks simultaneously. THE HONEST CAVEATS: transformer-based set prediction needs more training compute and data, converges more slowly than a well-tuned Mask R-CNN, and can be harder to debug (query behaviour is less interpretable than 'this proposal, this box'). For a small dataset with a tight schedule, Mask R-CNN or a U-Net-plus-postprocessing pipeline is often still the right engineering choice. THE META-POINT worth stating: the shift is an instance of a recurring pattern in vision - replacing hand-designed pipeline stages (anchors, NMS, proposal generation, heuristic fusion) with a learned end-to-end formulation, once the formulation and the data scale make it possible.

standard.q: How does DeepLab's dilated-convolution approach differ from U-Net's encoder-decoder, and when would you pick each?
standard.a: THEY SOLVE THE SAME PROBLEM DIFFERENTLY. Both must reconcile two conflicting needs: large receptive field (which requires downsampling, since receptive field grows geometrically with stride) and high output resolution (which downsampling destroys). U-NET'S ANSWER - DESTROY THEN RESTORE. Downsample aggressively (to 1/16 or 1/32), build rich semantics at low resolution, then upsample back through a decoder, using CONCATENATING SKIP CONNECTIONS at every scale to reinject the high-resolution detail that the encoder still holds in its early layers. The information that downsampling lost is recovered from the skips rather than reconstructed. DEEPLAB'S ANSWER - DON'T DESTROY IT. Stop downsampling early (output stride 8 or 16 instead of 32) and replace the later stride-2 stages with DILATED convolutions, which grow the receptive field by spacing the kernel taps apart - a 3x3 conv at rate 12 covers a 25x25 region with 9 weights. Then capture multi-scale context with ASPP (parallel dilated convs at several rates plus an image-level pooling branch) and use a light decoder (v3+) for final sharpening. Nothing needs to be restored because less was thrown away. THE TRADE-OFFS. COMPUTE AND MEMORY: DeepLab runs deep layers at 1/8 resolution, which is 4-16x more expensive per layer than running them at 1/32 - dilated approaches are compute- and activation-memory-hungry. U-Net's encoder gets cheap fast, and its cost is dominated by the decoder. So on the same budget, U-Net is generally the lighter design and DeepLab buys accuracy with compute. BOUNDARIES: both can be sharp, but they get there differently - U-Net's skips supply genuine high-frequency detail from early layers, while DeepLab preserves resolution but its features at 1/8 are still 8x coarser than the input, hence v3+'s added decoder. DATA EFFICIENCY: U-Net is famously strong with tiny datasets (its whole origin story), partly because the skips reduce what the decoder must learn. DeepLab's designs assume ImageNet-pretrained backbones and reasonable data volume. GRIDDING: dilation has a failure mode U-Net does not - a stack of same-rate dilated convs samples a sparse lattice, so some pixels never contribute, producing checkerboard-like gridding artifacts; the fixes are mixed/increasing rates (hybrid dilated convolution) or parallel rates as in ASPP. WHEN I WOULD PICK EACH. Choose U-NET when: the dataset is small (medical, scientific, industrial inspection); the input is not a natural photograph so ImageNet pretraining helps less; you need full-resolution output with a modest compute budget; or you are doing image-to-image regression rather than classification-per-pixel (denoising, super-resolution, diffusion). nnU-Net's continued dominance on medical benchmarks is strong evidence for this regime. Choose DEEPLAB-STYLE DILATION when: you have a strong pretrained backbone and enough data; the scenes are natural images with large scale variation (Cityscapes, PASCAL) where multi-scale context via ASPP is the differentiator; and you can afford deep layers at 1/8 resolution. IN PRACTICE THEY CONVERGED. DeepLabv3+ added an encoder-decoder with skips (a U-Net idea), and many U-Net variants add dilated convolutions in the bottleneck (a DeepLab idea). Most strong modern systems combine: a pretrained backbone, some dilation or multi-scale context module, a decoder with skips, and increasingly a transformer for global context. If asked what I would actually deploy today, I would say: start from a well-supported implementation (nnU-Net for medical, a SegFormer/Mask2Former or DeepLabv3+ baseline for natural images), because the training recipe and data pipeline will matter more than this architectural choice - and then measure boundary and region metrics separately to see which axis needs work.

standard.q: Segmentation masks are extremely imbalanced. Walk through the loss functions and training strategies you would use.
standard.a: THE PROBLEM, quantified. In a typical medical or defect-detection mask, foreground is 0.1-5% of pixels. Plain cross-entropy averages over all pixels, so 95-99.9% of the gradient comes from background pixels the model already classifies correctly. Two failure modes follow: the model collapses to predicting all background (99% pixel accuracy, zero utility), or it learns only the largest, easiest foreground regions and systematically misses small structures. LOSS FUNCTIONS, in the order I would reach for them. (1) CE + DICE, the standard default (and what nnU-Net uses). Cross-entropy gives stable, well-conditioned per-pixel gradients everywhere; soft Dice is a RATIO so it is invariant to how much background there is, and it directly optimizes the overlap metric you will report. A roughly equal weighting is a strong starting point. Dice alone can be unstable - its gradient is noisy and ill-behaved when the ground-truth mask is empty (hence the smoothing epsilon), which is why the combination beats either alone. (2) TVERSKY / FOCAL TVERSKY when the cost asymmetry matters. Tversky = TP/(TP + alpha*FP + beta*FN); setting beta > alpha (e.g. 0.7/0.3) penalizes MISSES more than false alarms, which is usually correct clinically - a flagged false positive costs a radiologist a few seconds, a missed lesion costs much more. Focal Tversky adds an exponent to concentrate on hard examples. This is the principled way to encode the decision's real cost structure into training rather than fixing it post hoc with a threshold. (3) FOCAL LOSS - down-weights easy pixels by (1-p)^gamma so the loss concentrates on hard ones, which in segmentation means boundaries and small objects. Useful in combination with Dice, particularly for extreme imbalance. (4) BOUNDARY-AWARE LOSSES - boundary loss, Hausdorff-distance surrogates, or simply weighting pixels near object boundaries higher (the original U-Net used a per-pixel weight map that upweighted the thin gaps between touching cells, which is what let it separate adjacent instances). Worth adding when boundary quality is the failure mode. (5) CLASS-WEIGHTED CE - simple inverse-frequency weighting. Crude (it upweights easy interior foreground pixels equally with hard boundary ones) and can destabilize training with extreme weights, but sometimes sufficient. TRAINING STRATEGIES, which often matter MORE than the loss. (a) FOREGROUND-BIASED PATCH SAMPLING: train on crops, and force a fixed fraction (commonly 1/3 to 1/2) of crops to be centred on a foreground voxel. This changes the effective class distribution the network sees without distorting the loss surface, and it is the single most effective intervention in most pipelines. (b) DOMAIN-APPROPRIATE AUGMENTATION: elastic deformation for anatomy, rotation/flip only where anatomically valid, intensity/contrast/gamma and modality-specific artifacts (bias field, noise). Augmentation is usually the largest source of gains in small-data segmentation. (c) HANDLE THE 'EMPTY MASK' CASE explicitly - images with no foreground at all break Dice and can dominate a dataset; decide whether to exclude them, include them with CE only, or use the smoothing term. (d) DEEP SUPERVISION: attach auxiliary losses at multiple decoder scales so gradients reach early layers directly and coarse predictions are supervised - a standard trick in nnU-Net and many detection/segmentation systems. (e) NORMALIZATION CHOICE: batch sizes in segmentation are tiny (large images), so BatchNorm statistics are unreliable - prefer GroupNorm or InstanceNorm, or use large-crop/small-batch with care. THRESHOLD AND POST-PROCESSING, which people forget: the operating threshold on the probability map is a DECISION parameter, not a fixed 0.5 - tune it on validation for the metric you care about (this alone can move Dice several points). Then remove tiny connected components below a size prior, fill holes, and if instances are needed, apply watershed on the distance transform to split touching objects. METRICS - report per-class IoU/Dice, precision and recall separately, boundary metrics, and the distribution over cases rather than only the mean; stratify by object size, because Dice punishes small objects far more for the same absolute error. THE ONE-PARAGRAPH SUMMARY: use CE + Dice (Tversky if false negatives cost more), sample patches with a foreground bias, augment aggressively in domain-valid ways, use GroupNorm and deep supervision, tune the decision threshold on validation, and evaluate with per-class and per-case metrics stratified by size - never a single mean number, and never pixel accuracy.

deepDive.q: Why can a model with excellent mean Dice still be clinically or operationally useless?
deepDive.a: Because mean Dice answers a question that is often not the question the system exists to answer, and it aggregates over exactly the axes where failure concentrates. Five distinct mechanisms. (1) IT AVERAGES OVER CASES, HIDING CATASTROPHIC FAILURES. A mean Dice of 0.85 is consistent with 0.90 on 90% of patients and 0.35 on 10%. In a screening context, those 10% are the entire risk. The fix is to report the DISTRIBUTION - median, interquartile range, worst-case, and the fraction of cases below a clinically acceptable threshold - not a single mean. This is the single most common reporting failure in segmentation papers and products. (2) DICE IS BIASED BY OBJECT SIZE. A 3-pixel boundary error on a 10,000-pixel organ is invisible to Dice; the same 3-pixel error on a 12-pixel micro-lesion destroys it. So averaging Dice across cases with varying object sizes conflates 'model is bad' with 'object is small', and a model that finds every large structure and misses every small one can post a strong mean. Small lesions are frequently the clinically important ones (early tumours, micro-calcifications). The fix is to stratify evaluation by object size and to use DETECTION-style metrics (sensitivity at a fixed false-positives-per-case) for small structures. (3) THE UNIT OF DECISION IS USUALLY NOT THE PIXEL. If the clinical question is 'is there a lesion, and where', the relevant metrics are LESION-LEVEL detection sensitivity and false positives per scan. A model can segment 85% of each lesion's pixels beautifully (high Dice) while missing 30% of lesions ENTIRELY (each missed lesion contributes one low-Dice case that the mean absorbs). Conversely a model can find every lesion but delineate them loosely, which is fine for detection and bad for volumetry. Always ask what number downstream actually consumes - volume, boundary, presence/absence, or count - and measure that. (4) REGION METRICS ARE NEARLY BLIND TO BOUNDARY ERRORS THAT MATTER. For radiotherapy planning or surgical navigation, a systematic 2 mm boundary offset toward a critical structure is dangerous, yet on a large organ it barely moves Dice. Hausdorff distance (95th percentile, to be robust to outliers), average symmetric surface distance, and boundary-F1 expose this; Dice does not. Conversely, Hausdorff is very sensitive to a single stray voxel, so the two families must be reported together. (5) THE TRAINING DISTRIBUTION IS NOT THE DEPLOYMENT DISTRIBUTION. Cross-validated Dice on one hospital's scanner says little about a different scanner, protocol, contrast agent, or patient demographic. Segmentation models are notoriously brittle to acquisition shift, and the failure is usually silent - the mask still looks plausible. Evaluate on genuinely EXTERNAL data (different site and scanner), and monitor input distribution in deployment. THE POSITIVE PRESCRIPTION: define the downstream decision first, then choose metrics that measure it - lesion-level sensitivity and FP/case for detection-like uses, volume error and its bias for quantification, surface distances for planning, and per-case distributions with worst-case reporting in all of them. Include an external validation set. And where possible, compare against the INTER-ANNOTATOR agreement on the same data: if two experts agree at Dice 0.82, a model at 0.85 is already at the noise ceiling and further Dice optimization is measuring label noise, not quality. That last comparison is the one that most often reframes a project - and being the person who asks for it is a strong signal in an interview.

standard.q: How does Mask R-CNN work, and what is RoIAlign fixing?
standard.a: THE ARCHITECTURE. Mask R-CNN (He et al., 2017) is Faster R-CNN plus a mask head. The pipeline: (1) a BACKBONE (ResNet + FPN) extracts multi-scale features; (2) the REGION PROPOSAL NETWORK slides over those features and proposes class-agnostic candidate boxes with objectness scores; (3) for each proposal, features are extracted from the corresponding region of the feature map at a fixed size (7x7 for the box head, 14x14 for the mask head) via ROIALIGN; (4) three PARALLEL HEADS run on those region features - a classifier (which class), a box regressor (refine the box), and a small FULLY-CONVOLUTIONAL MASK HEAD that outputs a 28x28 binary mask; (5) post-processing applies NMS and pastes each mask back into the image at its box location. THE KEY DESIGN DECISION in the mask head: it predicts K binary masks, ONE PER CLASS, and uses only the mask for the class the classifier chose, with a per-pixel SIGMOID and binary cross-entropy rather than a softmax across classes. Decoupling mask prediction from classification this way was measured to matter substantially - a softmax across classes forces masks to compete, which hurts. WHAT ROIALIGN FIXES. Its predecessor, RoIPool, extracted a fixed-size feature grid from a region by (a) rounding the region's continuous coordinates to the integer feature-map grid, and (b) rounding again when dividing the region into bins. On a feature map with stride 16, a box at x=127.3 maps to 7.96 in feature coordinates, which RoIPool rounds to 7 - an error of up to half a stride, i.e. up to 8 pixels in the original image. For BOX prediction that is tolerable (the box regressor compensates and IoU thresholds are coarse). For MASKS it is fatal: the extracted features are misaligned with the actual object by several pixels, so the predicted mask is systematically offset, and every mask inherits the error. ROIALIGN removes both roundings: it keeps the continuous coordinates, samples four points per bin at exact locations using BILINEAR INTERPOLATION of the neighbouring feature values, and averages (or maxes) them. No quantization anywhere. The paper reports this alone improved mask AP by roughly 10-50% relative depending on the setting, with the biggest gains at strict IoU thresholds - which is exactly the signature you would predict for a fix to a systematic spatial offset. The general lesson is worth stating: any time you sample features at continuous locations, quantizing the coordinates introduces a bias whose size is one stride, and whether that matters depends entirely on the spatial precision your output requires. The same reasoning appears in deformable convolutions, spatial transformers, and grid_sample-based warping. STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF MASK R-CNN. Strengths: accurate, well-understood, extremely well-supported (Detectron2, torchvision), naturally multi-task (boxes + masks + keypoints from one backbone), and it handles overlapping instances cleanly since each RoI is segmented independently. Limitations: the 28x28 mask resolution means large objects get coarse masks (PointRend was invented specifically to fix this by adaptively refining points along boundaries); the two-stage pipeline is slow relative to one-stage methods; it depends on NMS, which fails when objects heavily overlap; it inherits anchor hyperparameters; and the mask is confined to the detected box, so a missed or badly-fitting box caps mask quality - detection errors propagate. WHAT CAME AFTER. One-stage instance segmentation (YOLACT, SOLO/SOLOv2, CondInst) removed the proposal stage for speed. PointRend improved boundary quality by treating mask refinement as adaptive point sampling. And the mask-classification family (MaskFormer/Mask2Former) removed boxes and NMS entirely by predicting a set of masks with Hungarian matching - which is where the field is now. But Mask R-CNN remains the reference baseline and the thing most interviewers expect you to be able to draw, and RoIAlign is the detail that shows whether you understand why pixel-level tasks are harder than box-level ones.

standard.q: You need to segment 4000x4000 satellite images with a model trained on 512x512 crops. What problems arise and how do you handle them?
standard.a: This is a practical systems question and there are five distinct problems. (1) MEMORY - you cannot run the full image. A 4000x4000x3 image through a segmentation network produces activation maps far beyond GPU memory (the first layer alone at 64 channels is 4000*4000*64 = ~1 GB in fp32, and you need many such maps plus the decoder). So you must TILE: split into overlapping patches, predict each, and stitch. (2) BORDER ARTIFACTS - the central issue. A pixel near a tile edge has less context than a pixel in the tile centre, because part of its receptive field falls outside the tile and is replaced by padding. Predictions therefore degrade toward tile borders and you get visible SEAMS in the stitched output. The fixes, in increasing quality: use OVERLAPPING tiles and discard a border margin from each prediction (the margin should be at least half the receptive field); better, blend overlapping predictions with a WEIGHTED average using a window that is high in the centre and tapers to zero at the edges (a Gaussian or Hann window), which removes seams smoothly; best, do both and average probability maps rather than hard labels, then argmax at the end. Note that the required overlap is determined by the model's receptive field, which you should compute rather than guess. (3) SCALE AND CONTEXT MISMATCH - the subtler problem. A 512x512 crop of a 4000x4000 image may not contain enough context to disambiguate a class: a patch of dark texture might be water, shadow, or asphalt, and only the surrounding kilometre disambiguates it. Options: train at a lower resolution (downsample the image so one crop covers more ground, trading fine detail for context); use a MULTI-SCALE approach - run the model at two scales and fuse, or feed a downsampled global context branch alongside the high-resolution crop; or use a model with a genuinely large receptive field (dilated convolutions, or attention with global tokens). Also ensure the GSD (ground sample distance, metres per pixel) at inference matches training - satellite datasets mix sensors and resolutions, and a model trained at 0.5 m/px will silently fail at 2 m/px. (4) CLASS IMBALANCE AND SAMPLING - satellite scenes are dominated by a few classes (vegetation, water, background) with rare, important classes (a specific building type, a damaged structure) occupying a tiny fraction. During TRAINING, sample crops with a foreground bias rather than uniformly at random, or you will spend most batches on empty fields. During EVALUATION, report per-class IoU and be explicit that mIoU over 20 classes with 3 rare ones is dominated by the common ones. (5) THROUGHPUT AND ENGINEERING - a 4000x4000 image at 512 tiles with 25% overlap is ~100 forward passes; a country-scale mosaic is millions. So batch the tiles, use fp16 or int8, run with a data pipeline that overlaps I/O with compute (reading large GeoTIFFs is often the bottleneck, not the GPU), and process with a windowed reader (rasterio/GDAL) rather than loading whole scenes into RAM. Keep the georeferencing metadata attached so the output mask maps back to real coordinates - a very common source of silent bugs in geospatial pipelines. TWO MORE DOMAIN-SPECIFIC ISSUES worth raising because they show real experience: (a) SPECTRAL BANDS - satellite imagery often has more than 3 channels (NIR, SWIR), and ImageNet-pretrained backbones expect 3; either adapt the first conv (replicate/average pretrained weights across the extra bands) or accept training from scratch on the extra channels, and normalize per-band using dataset statistics, since raw radiance values are nothing like natural-image RGB. (b) TILING ARTIFACTS IN THE LABELS - if annotations were themselves made per-tile, label discontinuities exist at tile boundaries in the TRAINING data, and the model will learn them. VALIDATION STRATEGY: split geographically, never randomly - adjacent tiles are near-duplicates, so a random tile split leaks badly and can inflate scores by a wide margin. Hold out entire regions or scenes, and if possible a different sensor or season, since the real deployment shift is spatial and temporal.

standard.q: What is SAM (Segment Anything) and how has it changed segmentation practice?
standard.a: WHAT IT IS. SAM (Kirillov et al., Meta AI, 2023) is a PROMPTABLE, CLASS-AGNOSTIC segmentation foundation model. Architecture: a heavyweight ViT image encoder that runs ONCE per image producing an embedding; a lightweight prompt encoder that accepts points (foreground/background clicks), boxes, or coarse masks; and a very light mask decoder (a couple of transformer layers) that combines them to emit masks in milliseconds. That asymmetry is the design's key practical property - the expensive part is amortized over an interactive session, so a user can click repeatedly and get instant masks. It outputs THREE masks per prompt with confidence scores, deliberately, to handle ambiguity: a click on a person's shirt might mean the shirt, the torso, or the whole person, and rather than guessing, the model returns all three valid interpretations. THE DATA STORY IS THE REAL CONTRIBUTION. SAM was trained on SA-1B: 1.1 billion masks over 11 million images, built with a three-stage DATA ENGINE - annotators labelled with model assistance, the model improved, it began proposing masks automatically that annotators only corrected, and finally it generated masks fully automatically at scale. That bootstrapping loop, not the architecture, is the paper's central lesson: how to get to a billion masks when mask annotation is the most expensive labelling task in vision. WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT DO. SAM is CLASS-AGNOSTIC: it segments 'a thing' but does not tell you what the thing is. It has no semantic vocabulary of its own, so it is not a semantic-segmentation model and cannot replace one. Combined with a classifier or an open-vocabulary model (CLIP, Grounding DINO -> 'Grounded SAM'), it becomes text-promptable segmentation, which is how it is usually deployed for open-vocabulary tasks. HOW IT CHANGED PRACTICE. (1) ANNOTATION IS TRANSFORMED. This is the largest and most immediate effect: SAM-assisted labelling reduces mask annotation from minutes of careful polygon drawing to a couple of clicks per object, often an order of magnitude faster. Practically every modern annotation tool now integrates it. For a small-data project, the right first move is often 'use SAM to bootstrap masks, correct them, then train a task-specific model' - which changes the economics of starting a segmentation project. (2) ZERO-SHOT AND INTERACTIVE APPLICATIONS. Photo/video editing tools, robotics grasping (segment the object under the gripper), and AR object selection can now use segmentation without any task-specific training. (3) AS A COMPONENT, NOT AN ENDPOINT. SAM masks are used as proposals or priors inside larger systems - pseudo-labels for semi-supervised training, region proposals for open-vocabulary detection, or masks for downstream editing/inpainting pipelines. (4) IT DID NOT REPLACE SPECIALIZED MODELS, which is the honest and important caveat. On specialized domains - medical imaging, remote sensing, microscopy - vanilla SAM underperforms domain-trained models substantially, because SA-1B is natural images and those domains have very different statistics and notions of what constitutes an object; this drove a wave of adapted variants (MedSAM and many others) that fine-tune it on domain data. It is also class-agnostic, so any task needing semantics needs another model, and the ViT-H encoder is heavy for real-time or edge use (hence MobileSAM, EfficientSAM, FastSAM, and SAM 2 which extended it to video with a memory mechanism for tracking masks across frames). THE BROADER SIGNIFICANCE, and the answer I would give to 'why does this matter': SAM is the demonstration that the foundation-model recipe - a promptable interface, a task general enough to admit web-scale data, and a data engine to produce that data - transfers to a DENSE PREDICTION task, not just classification or language. The prompting interface is what makes it composable with other models, and the data engine is the transferable methodology. For a practitioner today, the practical takeaway is concrete: for a new segmentation project, evaluate SAM zero-shot as a baseline, use it to accelerate annotation regardless, and expect to fine-tune or train a specialist if your domain is not natural images.

flashcards.back: Semantic = class per pixel, no instances. Instance = separate object masks ('things' only, masks may overlap). Panoptic = both: every pixel gets a class, things also get instance ids - a complete non-overlapping partition.
IoU = TP/(TP+FP+FN). Dice = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN) = 2*IoU/(1+IoU), so Dice >= IoU always and they rank identically. Both ignore true negatives - which is why they survive imbalance.

flashcards.front: Never report pixel accuracy or mIoU alone
flashcards.back: All-background can score 99%. And the mean over classes hides catastrophic failure on the rare class you care about. Report per-class IoU, per-CASE distributions, and stratify by object size.

Gaps between kernel taps: a 3x3 at rate r covers (2r+1)x(2r+1) with 9 weights. Grows receptive field with no downsampling and no extra parameters. Uniform rates cause GRIDDING - use mixed/parallel rates (ASPP).

U-Net: downsample hard, then restore resolution via concatenating skips. DeepLab: don't downsample past 1/8, grow receptive field with dilation + ASPP. Dilation costs compute/memory; skips cost a decoder. They have since converged.

Bilinear sampling of RoI features WITHOUT rounding coordinates to the feature grid. RoIPool's double rounding misaligns by up to half a stride (~8 px at stride 16) - tolerable for boxes, fatal for masks.

A small FCN on each RoI predicting K binary masks (one per class), using per-pixel SIGMOID + BCE, taking only the classified class's mask. Decoupling mask from classification (no softmax across classes) measurably matters.

PQ = SQ x RQ: segmentation quality (mean IoU of matched segments) times recognition quality (F1 over segment matches at IoU>0.5). Cleanly factorizes 'found the right segments' from 'delineated them well'.

MaskFormer/Mask2Former predict a SET of (mask, class) pairs with Hungarian matching (DETR-style): semantic = merge same-class masks, instance = keep separate, panoptic = resolve overlaps. No anchors, no NMS, one architecture.

Border pixels lack context -> seams. Use overlapping tiles (overlap >= half the receptive field), blend probability maps with a tapered window, and split validation GEOGRAPHICALLY - adjacent tiles are near-duplicates and leak.
